title: Rumi of Konya
hook: Jalal al-Din Rumi, scholar of Konya, whose life turns when he meets Shams of Tabriz

segments.voice: Yesterday, al-Ghazali's crisis: the great scholar who could explain the path and hadn't tasted it. Your line was knowing is not tasting. What did you do instead of explain? Day two hundred ninety-eight.

You've probably seen his name on a mug, a poster or a wedding invitation. Rumi is often called one of the best-selling poets in America. But the man behind the quotes wasn't a greeting-card poet. He was a Muslim scholar, a preacher and a teacher of the law, in a city in the middle of what's now Turkey. He led prayers. He taught students. He was respected and settled. And then, in his late thirties, a wandering stranger walked into his life, and nothing about him was ever the same. Today, the scholar of Konya, and the meeting.
screen: `THE NAME ON THE MUG.` → `A SCHOLAR, A PREACHER, A TEACHER.` → `THEN A STRANGER ARRIVES.`

segments.voice: Jalal al-Din Muhammad was born in 1207, in the eastern Persian-speaking world, around Balkh. When he was a boy, his family moved west, just ahead of the Mongol invasions, and settled in Konya, in Anatolia. That region was called Rum, after the old Roman lands, and that's where his name comes from: Rumi, the one from Rum. Muslims often call him Mawlana, our master. His father was a preacher and scholar, and when his father died, Rumi took over his teaching. Then, in 1244, a wandering dervish named Shams, from Tabriz, arrived in Konya. The stories of their first meeting are many, and they're later legends; nobody knows exactly what happened. What's certain is what followed. The two became inseparable, talking for days on end. Rumi's students grew jealous. Shams left, came back, and then, a few years later, disappeared for good. Some said he was killed; the sources are unsure. Rumi searched for him and didn't find him. And out of that grief, the scholar became a poet. He composed thousands of verses of love poetry, and he named the collection after Shams. Later he dictated his great work, the Masnavi, full of stories and verses of the Qur'an. The Rumi on the mug is often stripped of all that. The early accounts describe a man who kept the prayers and the fasts, and his Masnavi draws on the Qur'an again and again. It all turned on one friend. The meeting.
screen: `BORN 1207, SETTLED IN KONYA.` · `RUMI — THE ONE FROM RUM.` · `SHAMS OF TABRIZ, 1244.` · `THE SCHOLAR BECOMES A POET.` · then, large: `THE MEETING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think of a friend who changed you. Sit, and breathe. Bring to mind one person who turned your life in a new direction. A teacher, a friend, a stranger for one afternoon, someone who asked the question nobody else asked. Picture their face. Remember what you were like before, and after. If they're alive, consider telling them. If they're gone, hold them for a moment with thanks. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. The bell holds the time.
Rumi of Konya. The Muslim scholar whose meeting with Shams of Tabriz turned him into one of the world's great poets. Today's word.
Your line: the meeting. Today, send one message to someone who changed you, and tell them how. Day two hundred ninety-eight.

howItsDone: Muslims across Turkey, Iran, Central and South Asia read Rumi's Masnavi as a work of Islamic spirituality, and every December many gather in Konya to mark the night of his death, which his followers call his wedding night with God.

original.note: Arabic, used in Persian and Turkish: our master, the title Rumi's followers gave him (Mevlana in Turkish).

what it means: a Muslim scholar whose meeting with Shams turned him into a poet of the love of God.
what a scholar hears: Jalal al-Din Rumi (1207–1273); Shams arrived in Konya in 1244; the Divan-i Shams and the six books of the Masnavi.
